content: The terminus of explanation is a philosophical problem, not a cognitive failing. Every chain of explanation ends in something unexplained, in a circle, or never; this is Agrippa's trilemma, and physicists who say the fundamental laws are brute facts are choosing the first horn, not lighting candles. Hume: "the most perfect philosophy of the natural kind only staves off our ignorance a little longer" (Enquiry IV.i, book, no DOI). By the essay's taxonomy, the physicist who accepts that the laws simply are has hit Ignore or Worship, and so has everyone who does not believe the regress goes on forever, which is nearly everyone. A three-button model that assigns every coherent stance on ultimate explanation to the two bad buttons has not described the options; it has renamed the problem.

quote: this question having never occurred to him before
content: No ethnographic record supports the wise man who has never wondered about rain. Foraging peoples maintain detailed causal meteorology, rainmaking practice and weather lore, and their supernatural accounts of rain coexist with practical prediction, as the sequence's own Belief in Belief would predict. More important, the cognitive science of religion holds that supernatural explanations do not arise from an explanatory drive at all: they are byproducts of agency detection and social cognition, intuitively compelling for reasons unrelated to their explanatory power (Boyer 2001, Religion Explained, book, no DOI; Barrett 2000). On that account the wise man did not hit Explain and get a bad answer; the "sky spirits" were never an answer to "why does it rain," and the essay's dialog-box model of the mind misdescribes what religious cognition is doing.
